prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Grandma is washing me white. I am the color of hot sand in the bleached sea light. I am a stain on the porcelain, persistent as tea. Stay in the shade. Don’t say she was the only one. Cousins opposite say: you too white. I am a night-blooming flower being pried open in the morning. My skin a curtain for a cage of bones, a blackbird coop. My heart is crusty bread, hardening. Hardening. This way, I feed my own fluttering. Under shade, the day looks like evening and I cannot bear the darkness. Don’t say, I can’t stand to be touched. Say, I stare into the sun to burn off the soiled hands that print my body with bloody ink. Don’t say, Mulatto. Say, I am the horse in Oz turning different colors, each prance brightening flesh. A curiosity. Don’t say, Bathwater spiraled down into the pipes. Say, I never did fade. Say, Skin holds the perseverance of my days. Folding, folding, the water continuously gathers, making wrinkles in a map.

Like tea that won't lift from china, I mark the porcelain and refuse to leave. Keep to the shadows. Don't mention that she stood alone. Across from me, my cousins declare I'm far too pale. # Caught Between Colors: A Journey Toward Self-Acceptance

From an early age, the narrator absorbed a painful and persistent message: that her skin was something to be corrected, lightened, made more acceptable. This pressure took on vivid, wounding forms in her memory—her grandmother scrubbing at her skin as if to wash her "white," and the constant admonitions to stay out of the sun and remain in the shade. These acts, perhaps intended as protection or care, communicated a deeper and more damaging idea: that her natural darkness was a flaw to be hidden or diminished.

Yet the narrator found herself trapped in an impossible position, caught between contradictory judgments that left no room for belonging. Within her own family, cousins accused her of being "too white," setting her apart as different, not quite one of them. At the same time, others reached for derogatory labels like "Mulatto," reducing her mixed-race identity to a slur. Whichever way she turned, she was measured against a standard she could never meet—too much of one thing, not enough of another, never simply herself.

The emotional toll of this constant judgment was profound. The narrator describes a deep and aching isolation, a sense of being fundamentally alone in her own skin. She evokes the image of bread left out too long, hardening and growing brittle—a metaphor for how she withdrew and closed herself off. Closeness became unbearable; she found herself shrinking from touch, unable to tolerate the very intimacy and connection that might have offered comfort. Her isolation was not only imposed from without but had taken root within.

But the narrator does not remain in this place of shame and retreat. Through an act of defiant reframing, she begins to reclaim her identity on her own terms. She refuses the shameful narratives that others have tried to write for her, rejecting the idea that her skin is something to apologize for or erase. Instead, she recasts herself as a source of vibrant wonder and fascination—comparing herself to the color-changing horse of Oz, a creature marvelous precisely because it defies a single fixed hue. In this reimagining, her complexity becomes not a burden but a marvel, something extraordinary rather than something wrong.

In the end, the narrator arrives at a powerful assertion of resilience and permanence. She declares that she never faded—that despite all the pressure to lighten and diminish, she has endured, whole and unchanged in her essential self. Her skin, far from being a mark of shame, becomes a testament to endurance, carrying within it the history and depth of everything she has lived through. It is not a flaw to be washed away but a lasting record of her survival, her strength, and her truth.
outputs.L4:
# The Weight of Water and Words

The poem opens on an intimate, wounding scene: a child held at a basin while a grandmother works soap and water into their skin, scrubbing as though color were dirt, as though brownness could be rinsed away. This is not the gentle bath of care but something more desperate—an act born of the grandmother's own inherited fears, her belief that lighter skin might spare the child the cruelties she has known. The imagery is deliberately visceral. We feel the roughness of the cloth, the sting of water, the raw sensation of being made to feel that one's very body is a problem to be corrected. The bristle and burn become physical proof of an emotional truth: that the speaker's identity has been marked, from the beginning, as something requiring erasure.

Throughout the poem, the speaker employs a recurring structure built on the commands "Don't say" and "Say." This call-and-response works like a catechism of self-definition. The "Don't say" lines carry the voices of shame—the internalized messages that name the speaker as lesser, as dirty, as unwanted. Against these, the "Say" lines rise up in resistance, offering a counter-language of dignity and endurance. The repetition mirrors the relentlessness of the scrubbing itself, but it also transforms it: what began as a rhythm of harm becomes a rhythm of reclamation. Each "Say" pushes back against each "Don't say," until the accumulated weight of the poem tips toward affirmation rather than injury.

At the heart of this tension lies the experience of colorism—the particular pain of being judged not only across racial lines but within them, of learning that gradations of skin can determine belonging. The mixed-race speaker occupies a space of doubled scrutiny, never quite passing, never quite fitting, subjected to the idea that they must be scrubbed toward whiteness to be acceptable. The grandmother, herself a product of a world that taught her these lessons, becomes both perpetrator and fellow victim, her hands enacting a violence she likely believed was love. This complexity keeps the poem from collapsing into simple accusation; instead, it holds grief and understanding together.

Yet the poem refuses to end in erasure. Its turn comes in the speaker's insistence: "I never did fade." The scrubbing failed. The color remained. What was meant as a mark of shame is reinterpreted as a mark of survival. The skin that could not be washed away becomes evidence of resilience, and the speaker reclaims it not as a burden but as a testament. When the poem declares that the skin "holds the perseverance of my days," it completes this transformation—the body is no longer a site of rejection but an archive of endurance, carrying the record of everything survived.

In the end, the poem converts a narrative of attempted destruction into one of triumphant persistence. The imagery that once conveyed pain now conveys strength; the repetition that echoed the scrubbing now echoes an anthem of self-worth. The speaker emerges not as someone diminished by the world's cruelty but as someone who has absorbed it, outlasted it, and claimed their own definition. What the grandmother could not scrub away, the speaker chooses to celebrate. Identity, the poem insists, is not something to be washed clean but something to be honored—held in the skin, written in the days, and spoken aloud in defiance of every voice that said it should fade.

# A Summer to Remember

Every year, when the school break arrived, young Don would pack his small suitcase and head out to the countryside to **stay** with his grandmother. It was a tradition that had begun before he could even remember, and it remained the highlight of his entire year.

**Grandma** lived in an old farmhouse at the end of a winding dirt road, surrounded by apple trees and a garden that seemed to stretch on forever. The moment Don stepped out of the car, she would wrap him in a warm hug that smelled of fresh bread and lavender.

"There's my favorite boy," she always said, cupping his face in her weathered hands. "Come now, Don, let's get you settled."

During his **stay**, the days passed slowly and sweetly. In the mornings, they would gather eggs from the chicken coop and pick ripe tomatoes from the vine. In the afternoons, Grandma taught him how to bake cookies, roll out dough, and tell stories the way she had learned from her own mother.

"Some things are worth learning slowly," she would remind him whenever he grew impatient. "The best memories are made when you take your time."

At night, Don would sit on the porch beside her, watching the fireflies dance across the field while she pointed out the constellations overhead. He never wanted those evenings to end.

When the summer finally drew to a close and it was time to leave, Don always felt a lump in his throat.

"Grandma," he whispered on his last day, "I wish I could **stay** forever."

She smiled gently and kissed his forehead. "You'll always have a home here, my dear. And I'll be counting the days until you return."

Years later, long after he had grown up, Don would still remember those precious summers—the laughter, the lessons, and the endless love of a grandmother who made every visit feel like coming home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about a mixed-race child being scrubbed clean by their grandmother, exploring colorism, skin, and belonging.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Washing

Grandmother's hands know only one temperature: hot enough to leave the truth pink and gasping. She works the washcloth in circles, as if my skin were a window she could see through if she only tried harder, as if beneath the brown there waited some cleaner version of a child she could love without the complication of my father's summer in it.

*You just need scrubbing*, she says, and I believe her the way you believe anyone who holds you naked in their lap. The water goes gray. Still I am myself. Still my knuckles keep their shadow, my elbows their dusk. She sighs the sigh of a woman who has been disappointed by weather, by men, by the stubbornness of pigment that will not surrender to soap.

I am six and already learning the arithmetic of belonging: how much lighter equals how much loved, the exchange rate of a face. My cousins run pale as communion wafers through her house and she does not reach for them with the rag. Only me. Only the one the sun claimed early, the one whose blood arrived by two directions and could not choose.

Here is what she cannot scrub away: the way I am a map of everywhere my mother wandered. The way my color is not dirt but *arrival*—generations traveling toward this particular brown, this exact and unrepeatable dusk of skin. Grandmother, I want to say, *I am not unfinished. I am not the smudge on your good name.*

But I am six. I let her wash me. I let her believe in the cleaner child beneath, that ghost she loves more than the boy in front of her. And when she is done and I am raw and holy with her failure, I look down at my own two hands—still brown, still mine, still glowing like something that refuses, that has always refused, to be anything but itself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical piece using the repeated structure "Don't say... Say..." that transforms shame about one's body and heritage into defiant imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# Don't Say, Say

Don't say *too much*—
Say *abundance*, say my grandmother's hands
kneaded bread from nothing
and I am the loaf that rose.

Don't say *dark*—
Say *dusk-skinned*, say *earth after rain*,
say the color the soil turns
when it's ready to grow something holy.

Don't say *loud*—
Say *unbroken*, say my mouth
is the last unmuted room
in a house they tried to silence.

Don't say *too wide, too soft, too much of you*—
Say *harbor*, say *horizon*,
say there is finally enough of me
to hold my own name.

Don't say *foreign*—
Say *fluent in two hungers*,
say my tongue carries a country
folded like a map inside the cheek.

Don't say *ashamed*—
Say *I inherited a spine*,
say *look how many storms
it took to bend it, and it did not break.*

Don't say *hide*—
Say *stand in the doorway*,
say let the light find every scar
and call each one a door I walked through.

Don't say *sorry* for the shape of me,
the sound of me, the roots of me—

Say *here*.
Say *whole*.
Say *mine.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem from the perspective of a light-skinned biracial person navigating family expectations, using vivid metaphors of bathwater, sunlight, flowers, and skin.
counterfactuals.output:
**Dilution Study, or: How to Read a Family in Water**

—

they say I came out
the color of *almost*

bathwater after the second child,
still warm    still holding somebody's soap

—

Grandmother measures me in flowers.
*You are the light one,* she says, meaning
the jasmine and not the soil it fed on,
meaning the petal
             and never
             the root's brown work below.

—

              in summer I am a negotiation.
              the sun comes for me like a relative
              I've never met—
              *finally,* it says, *finally you look like us*
              and I let it. I let it.
              I am always letting somebody
              claim the parts of me that surface.

—

here is the arithmetic they whisper:
    half of this
    half of that
    as if a person could be split
    down the sternum
    and both halves keep breathing.

—

Skin,
you traitor,
you translator,
you passport I never applied for—

you let me through doors
that swallowed my cousins whole,
and I stood in those rooms
              lighter
              lighter
holding the guilt like a wet towel
that will not wring dry.

—

              *You don't understand,* says one side.
              *You'll never understand,* says the other.
              and in the tub between them
              I am the water
              that took a little pigment
              from each hand that washed here
              and is asked, now,
              to run clear.

—

I am tired of being the *good* color.
I am tired of being the *proof*
that dilution is a kind of arriving.

—

Somewhere a flower opens
that is neither the mother's red
nor the father's gold
but a third thing—
              stubborn,
              unnamed in the family Bible,
              growing sideways out of the crack
              in everyone's expectation.

that one.
              call that one
              mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem about the trauma of being touched and the desire to burn away shame, weaving in themes of race, identity, and the color of skin.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Skin Remembers**

There is a map on my body
no one asked to draw—
fingerprints pressed like bruised ink
into the brown I was born wearing,
into the places I was told
were mine before they were taken.

They said my color was a warning,
a shadow that arrived
before I did.
And when hands came
uninvited as weather,
I learned to leave my own house,
to stand outside the door of my flesh
and wait for it to be over.

Shame is a second skin.
It fits too well.
It knows the shape of my shoulders,
the hollow of my throat,
the way I flinch
at kindness that comes too close.

I have wanted to burn it—
this inheritance of other people's guilt,
this catalog of touches
I never consented to keep.
I have wanted a fire
that takes only the shame
and leaves the girl,
that scorches the memory
but spares the brown,
the beautiful, unforgiven brown.

But listen:
my skin is not the crime.
My skin is the survivor.
It carried me through rooms
that wanted me smaller,
lighter, quieter, gone—
and still it holds me,
still it is the first home
and the last.

So let the burning be a cleansing,
not a vanishing.
Let me keep the color
and release the wound.
Let me touch my own arm
and feel only

*mine, mine, mine.*

---

Would you like me to adjust the tone, length, or lean more heavily into any particular theme?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, image-dense prose poem about a child being washed by their grandmother, referencing The Wizard of Oz's color-changing horse and the word "Mulatto."
counterfactuals.output:
**The Horse of a Different Color**

Grandmother dips the cloth and the whole kitchen tilts toward emerald. Water in the enamel basin goes the way of that Oz horse—first violet, then the yellow of a bruise remembering itself as gold, then a red she calls *good blood*, then no color the eye has a house for. She scrubs behind my ears where the dusk collects like flour.

*Mulatto*, she says, testing the word the way you test a stair in the dark, and it comes apart in the steam into *mule* and *little* and *auto*, a small engine hauling two fields that will not speak. The soap goes lavender, then the green of unripe seasons. My knees are two brown moons she polishes with her thumb until they remember being white bone underneath, until they remember being nothing at all, just an idea God had between two other, better ideas.

She pours the pitcher and my skin runs its whole carnival. See—I am the color of afternoon, then coffee left to the window, then the inside of a shell some ocean forgot to finish. The child in Oz kept changing and the guards just laughed, *that's the way we keep our streets*, painting the horse each hour so no one asks which stable it slept in. Grandmother laughs like that. She has painted me every hour of my life and still the neighbors squint.

The last of the water spirals down, taking a little of the emerald with it, a little of the me. She wraps me in a towel gone soft as a country that never existed. *You are not two things*, she says. *You are the whole basin. You are the color the water turns.*

And I climb out steaming into the ordinary kitchen, one boy, all my hues finally arriving at once, the horse at last standing still in a field with no color's name for its own, only the warm shape her hands have rubbed into being, only the clean, uncategorical dark of being held.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
